newsitem.title: USA: California governor backs $1.5 billion bridge plan.
newsitem.headline: California governor backs $1.5 billion bridge plan.

text.p: California Gov. Pete Wilson threw his weight Thursday behind a $1.5 billion plan to rebuild part of a 61-year-old San Francisco bridge rather than strengthen it to withstand earthquakes.

Wilson accepted the California Department of Transportation's recommendation to replace the eastern half of the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge, a key commuter route which carries an average of 280,000 vehicles a day.

"It is my belief that in order to best ensure the safety of motorists and the economic integrity of the (San Francisco) Bay area and the state, we should proceed with the construction of a new high-tech bridge to replace the aging Bay Bridge," Wilson, a Republican, said in a statement.
He said he had ordered California officials to begin an environmental review for replacing the bridge's eastern span.
The proposal calls for the eastern section of the bridge to be replaced with a two-mile (three-km) long steel-reinforced concrete skyway bridge with five traffic lanes in each direction.

The new section will link Yerba Buena Island, in the middle of San Francisco Bay, to Oakland. The existing western half of the bridge will remain in place and be strengthened to withstand earthquakes.
The Bay Bridge opened in 1936, a year before the Golden Gate Bridge. Although overshadowed by its world-famous neighbor, the Bay Bridge is a landmark of the area.

Engineers have been studying how to strengthen the Bay Bridge to better withstand earthquakes since a 50-foot (15-metre) section of the bridge collapsed in the devastating 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake.
State officials concluded that building a new eastern section would cost slightly more but be safer and more cost effective than strengthening it, known as "retrofitting."

Wilson and the state legislature must reach agreement on how to finance the project before construction can begin. State officials suggested the project could be funded through a mixture of highway funds, bonds and higher bridge tolls.
State engineers estimated that building a new eastern span and retrofitting the rest of the bridge would cost about $1.52 billion and that the new bridge could be open to traffic within seven years.
Just retrofitting the bridge would cost about $1.3 billion and take about five years to complete.

If the proposal is approved by state lawmakers and clears environmental hurdles, construction could start in 2000 and be finished by the end of 2003. Traffic would continue using the existing bridge until the new bridge opens.
